title: Grief becomes a verse
text: On the bank of the Tamasa a Nishada hunter shoots the male of a pair of krouncha birds at their loving. Valmiki hears the hen cry and a curse leaves his lips in four even feet of eight syllables. “What is this that I have uttered?” Out of shoka, sorrow, the shloka is born, and Brahma bids him tell Rama’s story in it.

title: Is there a man of all virtues?
text: Valmiki asks Narada who in this world is truthful, grateful, firm in his vows, master of his anger and yet terrible in battle. Narada answers with one name from the line of Ikshvaku: Rama, deep as the ocean, steady as the Himalaya, in valour like Vishnu and in forgiveness like the earth.

title: Ayodhya on the Sarayu
text: In the land of Kosala, on the bank of the Sarayu, stands the city Manu himself built: twelve yojanas long, its royal road sprinkled with water and strewn with flowers, ringed by a deep moat, crowded with elephants, horses and seven-storeyed mansions. Here Dasharatha rules as Indra rules Amaravati.

title: The gods ask Vishnu to be born a man
text: Ravana has Brahma’s boon that no god, gandharva, yaksha or rakshasa can kill him. In his contempt he never asked for safety from men. So the gods gather at Dasharatha’s sacrifice and beg Vishnu, who arrives on Garuda with conch, discus and mace, to divide himself in four and take birth as the king’s sons.

title: The vessel from the fire
text: Rishyashringa pours the oblation for sons, and out of the sacrificial fire rises a being of blazing radiance, dark, robed in red, with a lion’s mane, holding in both arms a golden vessel with a silver lid. “This payasam was made by the gods. Give it to your wives.” Dasharatha takes it like a poor man finding treasure, and shares it among Kousalya, Sumitra and Kaikeyi.

title: Four sons are born
text: In the twelfth month, in Chaitra, on the ninth lunar day, with five planets exalted, Kousalya bears Rama. Kaikeyi bears Bharata; Sumitra bears Lakshmana and Shatrughna. Gandharvas sing, apsaras dance, flowers fall from the sky, and Ayodhya’s streets fill with dancers and musicians.

title: Vishvamitra asks for Rama
text: “Give me Rama for ten nights. Maricha and Subahu foul my altar with flesh and blood.” Dasharatha, who has sworn to grant whatever the sage asks, turns faint: “My lotus-eyed Rama is not yet sixteen. Take me and my army instead.” Vishvamitra’s anger shakes the earth until Vasishtha persuades the king to keep his word.

title: Bala and Atibala, by the Sarayu
text: The two princes follow the sage, bows in hand, quivers on their backs, like two three-headed serpents. Half a yojana along the southern bank of the Sarayu, Vishvamitra says, “Rama, touch water,” and gives him the spells Bala and Atibala, so that neither hunger, thirst nor fatigue will touch him. They sleep that night on a bed of grass.

title: Tataka in the dead forest
text: The twang of Rama’s bowstring brings Tataka roaring out of the waste she has made of two rich provinces. She raises a storm of dust and rains boulders on the brothers. Rama, unwilling to kill a woman, first cripples her with arrows and Lakshmana cuts at her; when she vanishes into sorcery and dusk draws near, Vishvamitra says, “Enough pity.” One arrow through the chest ends her.

title: The weapons present themselves
text: Pleased with Tataka’s slayer, Vishvamitra faces east and gives Rama every celestial weapon he owns: the staff of Dharma, the wheel of Time, Vishnu’s discus, Indra’s vajra, Shiva’s trident, the Brahma-head. As he chants, the weapons arrive in shining bodies, join their palms and say, “We are your servants, Raghava.” Rama touches them: “Stay in my mind.”

title: Six nights’ watch: Maricha and Subahu
text: For six days and nights the brothers guard the altar without sleeping. On the sixth, the fire flares and the sky fills with rakshasas pouring down blood. Rama’s Manava weapon lifts Maricha and flings him a hundred yojanas, senseless, into the ocean; the Agneya burns through Subahu’s chest; the Vayavya sweeps away the rest. “I have done my teacher’s bidding.”

title: The descent of Ganga
text: On the way to Mithila the sage tells of Bhagiratha, who stood on the tip of one toe for a year so that Ganga might come down and wash the ashes of Sagara’s sixty thousand sons. Proud Ganga fell meaning to sweep Shiva into the underworld; he caught her in his matted hair and she wandered there for years before he let her down in seven streams.

title: Ahalya is seen again
text: Near Mithila stands an old hermitage, empty of sages. Here Goutama cursed his wife Ahalya, deceived by Indra, to lie for thousands of years on ashes, eating air, unseen by any creature, until Rama should come. As Rama steps in she becomes visible, blazing like a flame veiled in smoke. The brothers touch her feet; she welcomes them as guests, and Goutama returns to her.

title: Sita, risen from the furrow
text: Janaka tells his guests how he was ploughing the ground to clear it for a sacrifice when a baby girl rose from the furrow behind the ploughshare. He named her Sita, “furrow”, raised her as his own, and set her bride-price at valour alone: she would go to the man who could string the bow that Shiva left with his ancestors.

title: Rama breaks the bow of Shiva
text: Five thousand men drag in the iron casket on its eight wheels. With Vishvamitra’s leave Rama lifts the bow as if in play, strings it and draws; it snaps in the middle with a crack like a mountain splitting. The earth shakes and every man falls senseless, except Vishvamitra, Janaka and the two princes of Raghu’s line.

title: The wedding in Mithila
text: “This is Sita, my daughter. Take her hand in yours.” Janaka gives Sita to Rama before the fire that Vasishtha has kindled, and in the same hour Lakshmana weds Urmila, Bharata weds Mandavi and Shatrughna weds Shrutakirti. Flowers rain from the sky and the drums of the gods sound.

title: The other Rama
text: On the road home the sky darkens, birds scream and a whirlwind fells the trees. Out of it strides Rama of the axe, Jamadagni’s son, destroyer of kings, with Vishnu’s bow: “You broke Shiva’s old bow. String this one.” Dasharatha’s son takes it, strings it, fits an arrow, and the old warrior stands drained of his fire. The arrow is loosed on the worlds his austerities had won.

title: Seasons of love in Ayodhya
text: The brides come home to Ayodhya. For many seasons Rama lives with Sita, his mind always on her, his heart given over to her. She is dear to him because his father chose her; dearer still for her virtues and her beauty. Her husband lives twice over in her heart, and each knows without speaking what the other’s heart is saying.

title: The prince the people love
text: Valmiki pauses to describe him: Rama never speaks first in anger and answers harshness gently; he remembers one kindness and forgets a hundred wrongs; he sits with the old to learn, and in archery not even his father is his equal. When Dasharatha asks the assembly whom they want as heir, they answer with one voice, and tell the king why.

title: Manthara climbs to the roof
text: From the palace roof Kaikeyi’s old servant sees the streets watered, the flags up, the brahmanas with garlands. A nurse tells her why: tomorrow Rama is made heir. She runs to Kaikeyi, who gives her a jewel for the good news. Manthara throws it down. “Fool. Kousalya’s son rises and yours becomes his servant.” By nightfall the queen’s joy has turned.

title: Two boons
text: Dasharatha finds his youngest queen on the bare floor of the anger chamber, her ornaments flung off like stars fallen from the sky. He swears by Rama to give whatever she asks. She asks: let Bharata be consecrated with what has been made ready for Rama, and let Rama go to the Dandaka forest for fourteen years in bark and deerskin. The king falls like a tree cut at the root.

title: No change in his face
text: Summoned on the morning of his consecration, Rama finds his father silent and withered and hears the sentence from Kaikeyi instead. He does not flinch. “So be it. I will go to the forest in matted hair and bark, to keep the king’s promise. I have no wish to live for wealth; know me to be like the sages, devoted to dharma alone.” Those who watch see no change in his face.

title: “With you it is heaven”
text: Rama tells Sita to stay and serve his mothers. He lists the forest’s terrors: lions, thorns, snakes that move like rivers, hunger, the wind at night. She answers, first in love and then in anger: “A wife shares her husband’s fate. With you it is heaven; without you it is hell. I will walk ahead and crush the thorns.” He yields: “I did not know your whole heart.”

title: Lakshmana’s anger
text: “The king is old, besotted and in a woman’s grip. Before anyone hears of this, take the kingdom; I will stand beside you with my bow and kill whoever sides with Bharata, even our father.” Kousalya begs Rama not to leave her. Rama holds his brother’s wrist: “It is not in my power to cross my father’s word. Give up this ignoble thought. Dharma is the highest thing in the world.”

title: Bark for a princess
text: Kaikeyi herself brings the bark. Rama and Lakshmana lay aside their fine cloth and put it on. Sita, in silk, holds her piece like a doe looking at a snare and asks her husband how forest sages wear it; he ties it over her silk with his own hands. The women of the palace cry out, and Vasishtha turns on Kaikeyi: “Sita was no part of your boon.”

title: Leaving Ayodhya
text: Sumantra brings the chariot. Sita mounts first, then the brothers with their bows, swords and armour. The whole city runs after them, hanging on the sides: “Hold the horses. Let us see his face.” The old king stumbles out on foot with Kousalya, crying “Stop!” while Rama says “Drive on.” The dust the people’s tears had laid rises again behind the wheels.

title: The night on the Tamasa
text: The townspeople will not turn back; old brahmanas with heads white as swans walk behind the chariot. They all camp on the bank of the Tamasa. Rama drinks only water. Before dawn, while the people sleep, he wakes Sumantra: they drive north first to confuse the trail, then double back. The citizens wake to wheel-ruts that lead nowhere.

title: Guha keeps watch
text: At Shringaverapura on the Ganga, Guha, king of the Nishadas and Rama’s friend, comes with food and bedding. Rama embraces him but takes only water, and fodder for his father’s horses. He and Sita sleep on the ground under an ingudi tree. Lakshmana will not lie down. All night he and Guha stand with their bows, talking of the prince who should be on a palace bed.

title: Crossing the Ganga
text: At daybreak the brothers ask for the milky sap of a banyan and twist their hair into the matted locks of ascetics. Sumantra begs to come; Rama sends him back to comfort the king. In midstream Sita joins her palms: “Goddess Ganga, bring him home after fourteen years and I will worship you with a hundred thousand cows.” On the far bank they walk in file, Lakshmana ahead, Sita between.

title: Where two rivers meet
text: Smoke rising where Ganga meets Yamuna tells them they have reached Prayaga and the hermitage of Bharadvaja. The sage asks them to stay; Rama fears the townsfolk would find him so near, and asks for a lonelier place. “Ten krosha on: Chitrakuta.” The brothers lash logs and bamboo into a raft, lay a seat of reeds for Sita, and cross the dark Yamuna; she bows to the great fig tree on the far bank.

title: Chitrakuta: “I do not miss the city”
text: Rama shows Sita the mountain, its veins of mineral red and silver, its mango and jambu and flowering asana, kinnaras at play in the caves; then the Mandakini with its swans and sandbanks. “Bathing in this river thrice a day, eating honey and roots, with you beside me and Lakshmana at hand, I do not long for Ayodhya or the kingdom. Think of the mountain as the city and the river as the Sarayu.”

title: The arrow in the dark
text: On the sixth night after Rama left, Dasharatha tells Kousalya what he has hidden all his life. As a young prince proud of shooting by sound, he heard a gurgle on the Sarayu’s bank at night and loosed an arrow at what he took for an elephant drinking. It was a boy ascetic filling a pot for his blind parents. The old father’s curse: “You too will die grieving for a son.”

title: “Rama… Kousalya… I cannot see”
text: Past midnight, with the two queens beside him, the king’s breath stops on his son’s name. At dawn the bards come as always to sing him awake, and the women who touch his bed find it cold. The palace that had been all drums and song the week before fills with one long cry; the body is laid in a vat of oil until Bharata can come.

title: Bharata refuses a kingdom
text: Called home from his grandfather’s city with no reason given, Bharata rides into an Ayodhya without drums, garlands or swept streets. His mother greets him as king and tells him how she arranged it. “Murderess of your husband! You have dug a hole for our whole line. I will bring my brother back and be his servant.” Shatrughna drags Manthara across the floor until Bharata stops him.

title: Brothers at Chitrakuta
text: Bharata leaves the army a krosha off and climbs on foot. He sees the hut, the bows gleaming like rainbows, the altar; and Rama on the ground in black antelope skin with matted hair. He runs, stumbles, and cannot get past the word “Arya”. Rama lifts him onto his lap and asks first of all after their father. Then he hears the answer.

title: The sandals rule
text: Rama will not break their father’s word, and Bharata will not take the throne. So Bharata sets down a pair of gold-worked sandals: “Step on these.” Rama does, and hands them back. Bharata carries them on his head to Nandigrama, sets them on the throne under the white umbrella, and for fourteen years, in bark and matted hair, reports every act of state to them first. “If you are not back the day the term ends, I will enter fire.”

title: Anasuya’s gifts
text: Too many memories crowd Chitrakuta now, so they move south to the hermitage of Atri. His wife Anasuya, so old she trembles like a plantain in the wind, takes Sita aside, praises her for following her husband, and gives her a garland that will not fade, garments, ornaments and a salve. Sita tells her the story of her own wedding until the sun sets and the birds come home.

title: Viradha seizes Sita
text: Hardly inside the Dandaka forest, a rakshasa tall as a hilltop blocks the path, wrapped in a bloody tiger skin, three lions and four tigers spitted on his spear. He snatches Sita into his arms: “Two ascetics with one woman? She will be my wife.” Weapons cannot kill him by Brahma’s boon, so the brothers break his arms and bury him alive in a pit, as he himself asks.

title: The vow in Dandaka
text: The sage Sharabhanga, having seen Rama, enters his own fire and rises young to Brahma’s world. Then ascetics of every order gather: those who live on moonbeams, on water, on leaves, who stand in rivers. They show him a white hill of bones. “These were sages, eaten by rakshasas along the Pampa and the Mandakini. You are our king, even here.” Rama answers: “I came for my father’s word; I stay for yours.”

title: Agastya’s armoury
text: Ten years pass among the hermitages. Then they come to Agastya, who once drank the ocean and made the Vindhya mountain bow. The small sage rises to meet his guest and hands him what the gods left in his keeping: Vishnu’s bow, worked in gold and diamonds by Vishvakarma, the unfailing arrow of Brahma, two quivers that never empty, and a sword in a golden sheath. “Live at Panchavati, two yojanas on.”

title: Jatayu, and a house at Panchavati
text: On the road they meet a vulture so vast they take him for a rakshasa. “Child, I am Jatayu, your father’s friend. This forest is thick with night-rangers; I will watch over Sita when you and Lakshmana are away.” At Panchavati, where the Godavari runs through lotuses, Lakshmana raises a hut of clay walls, bamboo rafters and thatch. Rama embraces him: “In you, our father lives.”

title: Shurpanakha falls in love
text: Ravana’s sister, wandering the wood, sees Rama and is struck by desire. Valmiki sets them side by side: his face fair, hers foul; his waist slim, hers a pot; his hair fine, hers copper wire; his voice sweet, hers a croak. “I am Shurpanakha, who takes any shape she likes. Leave this sunken-bellied human. I will eat her, and you and I will roam Dandaka together.”

title: The sword at Panchavati
text: Mocked back and forth between the brothers, she decides the rival must go and rushes at Sita like a meteor at a star. Rama stops the game at once. “Never jest with the cruel. Lakshmana, mark this one.” Lakshmana draws his sword and takes off her ears and nose. She runs howling into the forest, arms thrown up, to her brother Khara and his fourteen thousand.

title: One against fourteen thousand
text: Khara marches from Janasthana with Dushana, three-headed Trishiras and fourteen thousand rakshasas, under a red sky with jackals howling. Rama sends Lakshmana to a cave with Sita and stands alone. Gods and sages crowd the sky to watch. He draws arrows so fast no one sees his hand move; in the time it takes to milk a cow, the host is down. Last comes Khara, mace in hand, and an arrow given by Indra.

title: Dashagriva on the throne of Lanka
text: Shurpanakha flies across the sea and finds her brother on a golden seat on the roof of his palace, blazing like a fire fed with ghee: ten necks, twenty arms, a chest scarred by Indra’s thunderbolt and the tusks of Airavata. “You sit drunk among your women while one man on foot has emptied Janasthana. And he has a wife, Ravana, such as no god or gandharva has.”

title: Ten heads, ten vices
text: Valmiki’s Ravana is no fool: a scholar of the Vedas, an ascetic who offered his own heads to Brahma, a king whose city is the wonder of the world. Tradition has read his ten heads as the ten appetites that ruled that learning: lust, anger, delusion, greed, pride, envy, selfishness, injustice, cruelty and ego. On the tenth day of the autumn festival all ten are burnt in effigy.
aside: The ten vices are a later devotional reading, not Valmiki’s; he calls him only Dashagriva, the ten-necked

title: Maricha sees Rama in every tree
text: Ravana crosses the sea in his mule-yoked sky-chariot to an ashram on the far shore where Maricha, once flung a hundred yojanas by a boy’s arrow, lives on roots in bark and black antelope skin. “Go back. I see Rama behind every tree, a thousand Ramas, bow in hand. Words that begin with the letter ‘R’, ratna, ratha, frighten me.” Ravana gives him a simpler choice: die there by Rama, or here by me.

title: The golden deer
text: It grazes by the hut: hide of gold flecked with silver, antler-tips of sapphire, belly pale as a lotus petal, nibbling shoots and glancing back. Sita, gathering flowers, has never wanted anything so much: alive as a playmate, or its skin to sit on. Lakshmana says flatly, “No such deer exists. That is Maricha.” Rama takes his bow: “Then I will kill Maricha. Guard her until I return.”

title: “Ah, Sita! Ah, Lakshmana!”
text: The deer shows itself and vanishes, draws him on, lets him near, bounds away, until the hut is far behind. Out of patience, Rama fits the arrow Brahma made. It splits the deer’s heart. Maricha leaps the height of a palm tree, falls in his own vast shape, and with his last breath does what he was sent to do: he cries out in Rama’s voice.

title: Words like heated arrows
text: “Go! That was your brother.” Lakshmana does not move: no one in the three worlds can harm Rama; the voice is sorcery. Then Sita, frantic, says the unforgivable: that he hangs back because he wants her, that he is Bharata’s spy. He covers his ears. “May the gods of the forest protect you, wide-eyed one. The omens are terrible.” There is no line drawn on the ground in Valmiki; he simply bows and goes.

title: The mendicant at the door
text: The moment Lakshmana is gone, Ravana steps out as a wandering ascetic: ochre robe, topknot, umbrella, sandals, staff and water pot. The wind drops; the leaves stop moving; the quick Godavari slows in fear. He praises her, limb by limb, in a way no holy man would. Sita, bound by the law of hospitality, offers him a seat and water for his feet, and keeps glancing at the forest path.

title: Ravana throws off the disguise
text: “I am Ravana, lord of Lanka, before whom gods tremble. Be my chief queen; five thousand women will serve you.” Sita answers that he is a jackal asking for a lioness, a man trying to pocket the sun. He strikes his palms together and the ascetic is gone: ten heads, twenty arms, eyes red as copper, in a robe the colour of blood, tall as a blue thundercloud over the leaf hut.

title: Sita is carried into the sky
text: With his left hand he seizes her by the hair, with his right beneath the thighs, and lifts her onto the golden chariot that has come at his thought, mules braying. It climbs. “Rama! Lakshmana! Trees of Janasthana, river Godavari, deer and birds, tell Rama!” Her anklet falls like lightning; flowers shower from her hair; the lotuses droop, the sun dims, and the wind itself seems to say there is no dharma left.
aside: Valmiki’s Ravana carries her off in a golden sky-chariot “like a vimana”, yoked to mules; the Pushpaka itself appears in paintings 80 and 100

title: Jatayu against Ravana
text: “I am sixty thousand years old, Ravana, and you are young, armed, in a chariot. You will not take her while I live.” The old vulture tears the armour from him, snaps two bows, kills the mules, pulls down the charioteer, smashes the car and its royal umbrella, and rips ten arms from his left side; they grow back like snakes from an anthill. Ravana drops to the ground with Sita on his hip and draws his sword.

title: Jatayu falls
text: The sword takes his wings, then his feet, then his flanks. The king of birds drops to the forest floor like a great tree, with a little life left in him. Sita runs to him and holds him as she would her own kin, crying. Ravana comes for her again; she clings to the trunks of trees. He takes her by the hair and rises, and Brahma, watching, says only: “It is done.”

title: A bundle of jewels
text: Chariot gone, Ravana flies south with Sita in his arms, a yellow streak of silk across his dark body like lightning on a cloud. Over a mountain she sees five great monkeys sitting on the peak. With no one else to tell, she strips off her ornaments, knots them in her upper cloth, and lets the bundle fall among them. In his hurry he does not notice. They watch, unblinking, until she is out of sight.

title: Twelve months
text: In Lanka he walks her through halls of ivory, crystal and gold. “All this, and I, are yours.” Sita sets a blade of grass between them and speaks to that instead of to him: “You have stolen Rama’s wife as a dog steals the offering. You are already dead.” Ravana names his term. “Twelve months. After that the cooks will cut you up for my morning meal.” The rakshasis lead her to the ashoka grove.

title: Rama asks the trees
text: The hut is empty. He runs from tree to tree: “Kadamba, have you seen her who loved your flowers? Bilva? Arjuna? Ashoka, remover of sorrow, remove mine.” He asks the deer, the elephant, the tiger. He asks the Godavari, and the river, afraid of Ravana, says nothing. Then the deer rise together, turn their faces south, and look up at the sky. Lakshmana understands them first.

title: Funeral rites for a bird
text: They find Jatayu dying and Rama, half-mad, takes him for the one who ate her. The bird speaks with blood in his throat: “Ravana took her, and my life. South.” He dies with the name on his beak. Rama, who could not perform his own father’s last rites, builds the pyre himself and gives the vulture what a son gives: fire, the offering of food, and water at the Godavari.

title: Kabandha
text: A thing with no head and no neck: a trunk like a storm cloud, a fanged mouth in its belly, one fiery eye in its chest, and arms a yojana long that rake the forest for food. It has both brothers in its fists before they see it. They shear the arms off at the shoulder. Burnt at his own request, he rises as a shining gandharva: “Find Sugriva on Rishyamuka, by Pampa. Make him your friend before the fire.”

title: Shabari has waited
text: On the western shore of Pampa an old woman of the forest people has kept a hermitage alone since her teachers, the disciples of Matanga, rose to heaven. They told her Rama would come. She touches the brothers’ feet, sets before them the fruits and roots she has gathered along the lake, and shows them the grove: altars still warm, garlands unfaded. Then, with his leave, she walks into her fire and goes to her teachers.

title: Spring on Pampa
text: The lake is clear as crystal, red, white and blue with lotuses, loud with geese; the wind off the Malaya hill shakes flowers down like rain. For a man alone it is unbearable. “Look, Lakshmana: the peacock dances and his hen dances after him. No rakshasa has carried off his love. Go back to Bharata. I cannot live without her.” On the hill above, a monkey king sees two armed men and trembles.

title: Hanuman comes down the mountain
text: Sugriva sends his minister to find out who the two archers are. Hanuman puts off his monkey shape for a mendicant’s, bows, and speaks: who are you, with arms like gate-bars and bows like rainbows, lighting up this shore? Rama turns to Lakshmana, delighted. “No one who has not mastered the three Vedas speaks like this. Not one word out of place, not a flaw in his face as he says it.”

title: Friendship before the fire
text: Hanuman takes his own form again and carries the brothers up Rishyamuka on his shoulders. Sugriva holds out his hand: “If you want my friendship, here is my arm.” Hanuman twirls two sticks into flame; Rama and the monkey king walk round it and are bound. They sit together on a branch of flowering sala. In that moment, the left eyes of Sita, of Vali and of Ravana begin to throb.

title: “I know the anklets”
text: Sugriva fetches from the cave a yellow cloth knotted round a handful of jewels: “A woman carried through the sky dropped this among us, crying ‘Rama’.” Rama holds it to his chest and cannot see for tears. “Lakshmana, look. Are these hers?” “I do not know the armlets, nor the earrings. The anklets I know, from bowing at her feet every day.”

title: One arrow, seven trees
text: Sugriva still doubts: Vali once hurled the corpse of the buffalo-demon Dundubhi a full yojana, and could shake seven great sala trees at once. Rama tips the dry skeleton with his toe and sends it ten yojanas. Then he draws. The gold-shafted arrow passes through all seven trunks, through the mountain behind them, down through the earth, and comes back to his quiver.

title: Two brothers, one face
text: Sugriva roars at the gate of Kishkindha and Vali comes out like the sun over a hill. They fight with fists, knees, trees and rocks, alike as the twin Ashvins, and Rama, arrow on the string, cannot tell which to shoot. Sugriva limps back, beaten and bitter. Lakshmana winds a flowering gajapushpi creeper round his neck, and he goes to roar again. Tara begs her husband not to answer it.

title: Vali’s question
text: The arrow takes him in the chest and he falls like Indra’s banner cut down, the golden garland still holding his breath and splendour in him. “I was fighting another. What dharma is this, Rama, to shoot from hiding?” Rama answers him as a king answers: for the brother’s wife he took. Vali listens, and yields. He gives the garland to Sugriva and his son Angada into Rama’s keeping. Tara will not let go of him.

title: The rains on Mount Malyavat
text: Sugriva is crowned and the monsoon closes the roads. Rama and Lakshmana wait it out in a cave. “The sky has drunk the sea through the sun’s rays for nine months and now gives birth. One could climb to the sun on that stair of clouds. See the lightning writhe in the dark cloud’s arms, as Vaidehi must in Ravana’s.” Four months of rain; every night of it he counts.

title: Autumn, and a broken promise
text: The skies clear, the rivers show their sandbanks, and no army comes. Sugriva is drunk in his inner rooms with Ruma and Tara. Lakshmana walks into Kishkindha with his bow strung; the twang of it sobers the king at once. Sugriva sends Tara out first, unsteady, her girdle loose. “Even sages lose themselves to desire; forgive a monkey. The call has already gone to every mountain.”

title: A ring with his name on it
text: They come like clouds: monkeys white as the moon, red as the dawn, dark as rain, in tens of millions from Himalaya, Vindhya and the sea-coast. Sugriva sends them out to the four quarters, a month to search. The south goes to Angada, Jambavan and Hanuman. Rama draws from his finger the ring engraved with his name and gives it to Hanuman. “By this she will know you came from me.”

title: Sampati looks across the sea
text: The month is spent and the southern party has found nothing but the shore. They lie down on darbha grass to starve rather than face Sugriva. A huge wingless vulture creeps from a cave, glad of the meal, and hears them name Jatayu. “He was my younger brother. I burnt my wings shielding him from the sun.” With a vulture’s sight he looks south: “A hundred yojanas. Lanka. She sits there in yellow silk, among rakshasis.”

title: Jambavan rouses Hanuman
text: Who can leap a hundred yojanas? One says ten, another thirty, ninety; Angada could cross but not return. Hanuman sits apart, silent. Old Jambavan turns to him: “Why do you say nothing? You are the Wind’s son. As a child you leapt at the sun for a fruit and Indra’s bolt broke your jaw; that is your name.” Hanuman remembers himself, and begins to grow.

title: The leap
text: He crouches on Mahendra and the mountain sweats water and red ore; snakes spit fire from its caves; sages rise into the air to watch. Then he is gone. Trees torn up by the wind of his thighs follow him out to sea like kin seeing off a traveller, and their flowers fall on the water like stars. His shadow lies on the waves ten yojanas wide and thirty long.

title: A mountain rises to offer rest
text: The Ocean owes the house of Ikshvaku a debt, and bids the golden mountain hidden in his depths to rise. Mainaka stands up through the waves, peaks blazing, and speaks in a man’s shape from his summit: “Rest on me. Your father the Wind once saved me when Indra was cutting the wings off the mountains.” Hanuman touches him with his palm. “I have promised not to stop on the way.”

title: Surasa’s mouth
text: The gods want to see what he is made of, and send Surasa, mother of serpents, to stand in his path as a rakshasi: “No one passes me without entering my mouth.” He grows; her jaws grow wider. Ten yojanas, twenty, fifty, ninety, a hundred. Then he shrinks to the size of a thumb, darts in and out between her teeth, and bows in mid-air. “I have entered your mouth. Farewell.”

title: The shadow-catcher
text: Something has hold of him; he flies like a ship against the wind. Below, a huge shape lifts from the water with his shadow in its grip. This is Simhika, of whom Sugriva warned, who eats what she catches by its shadow. Her mouth opens like the underworld. He makes himself small as a bolt, drops into it, tears out her heart with his nails, and is up in the sky again before she sinks.

title: Lanka by moonlight
text: He lands on the Trikuta peak and looks: walls of gold, gateways of lapis and crystal, moats thick with lotuses, banners like creepers, a city hung in the sky. No army could take it. He waits for the sun to set, makes himself small, and steps onto the rampart with his left foot first. The moon comes up as if to light his way, white as a conch, like a swan in a silver cage.

title: The sleeping palace
text: He searches house by house and comes to Ravana’s own, and in it the Pushpaka, the flying palace taken from Kubera, built by Vishvakarma, moving at its master’s thought. Past midnight the great hall is a lotus pond of sleeping women, drums and vinas dropped beside them. Ravana sleeps like a dark cloud on a crystal dais. Seeing Mandodari, golden and jewelled, Hanuman leaps for joy: Sita! Then he thinks again. Sita would not sleep.

title: Under the shimshapa tree
text: Only the ashoka grove is left unsearched. From the top of a golden-leaved shimshapa he sees her at last: thin with fasting, in one worn yellow cloth, on the bare ground, sighing; like the sliver of the new moon, like a flame wrapped in smoke, like a doe strayed from the herd among hounds. Round her squat the guards: one-eyed, one-eared, ears like winnowing fans, faces of boar and camel.

title: Ravana comes before dawn
text: In the last watch of the night, woken by the chanting of his brahma-rakshasas and by the thought of her, Ravana comes with a hundred women carrying lamps of scented oil, fans and a gold pitcher. Sita covers herself with her knees and arms. He pleads, boasts, offers; she answers through a blade of grass. “Two months remain,” he says, and raises his hand to strike. A young queen draws him away, laughing.

title: Trijata’s dream
text: When he has gone the guards close in: “Marry him, or we share you out for breakfast.” Sita looks for a rope, and thinks of her braid. Then old Trijata wakes. “Eat me instead. I have dreamed: Rama in white garlands on a chariot of ivory drawn by swans, Sita standing on a white hill in the sea. And Ravana, shaven, in red, drinking oil, riding a donkey south. Lanka fell into the ocean.”

title: Hanuman gives her the ring
text: How to speak without frightening her? From the branch, softly, in human speech, he tells the story of Dasharatha’s son: the exile, the deer, the search. She looks up and sees a small monkey the colour of ashoka flowers, and fears another trick of Ravana’s. He comes down, palms joined, and describes Rama mark by mark. Then: “See, this ring bears his name.” She takes it, and it is as if she had her husband’s hand.

title: The crest-jewel
text: “Climb on my back; I will carry you over the sea tonight.” She smiles at the little monkey, and he shows her his real size, a mountain with copper face and diamond teeth. Still she refuses: let Rama come, kill Ravana and take her back himself; that alone is worthy of him. She unties from her cloth the jewel she wore in her hair, and tells a secret only Rama knows: the crow at Chitrakuta, and the blade of grass.

title: The grove destroyed
text: Conciliation, gifts and division are no use with rakshasas; that leaves force, and a look at their strength. He tears up the pleasure-grove, tree by tree, sparing only Sita’s, and takes his stand on the gateway with an iron bar. “Victory to Rama! I am Hanuman, servant of the king of Kosala.” Eighty thousand guards, Jambumali, seven ministers’ sons, five generals. Then Ravana sends his own boy, Aksha, in a chariot with eight horses.

title: The envoy in ropes
text: Indrajit binds him with Brahma’s weapon; Hanuman, who has that god’s promise it will hold him only a moment, lets himself be led, to see Ravana and speak. And seeing him he thinks: what form, what steadiness, what splendour. Were it not for his adharma he could be guardian of heaven. He delivers Rama’s message. Ravana orders him killed. Vibhishana stands: “An envoy is never put to death.”

title: Lanka burns
text: “Monkeys prize their tails. Burn it and send him home.” They wrap it in oiled rags and parade him through the streets, which suits him: he studies the fortifications. Sita, told of it, prays to the fire: “If I have been faithful, be cool to Hanuman.” The flame burns cold on him. He slips his ropes, leaps to a rooftop, and goes house to house with his tail alight, sparing only Vibhishana’s.

title: “Seen: Sita”
text: The southern party comes home roaring, and wrecks Sugriva’s honey-grove on the way for sheer joy. Hanuman bows to Rama and says the important word first: “Seen. I have seen the lady.” He lays the jewel in his hand. Rama holds it against his chest and weeps. “This was her father’s gift at our wedding. I have nothing to give that matches what you have done. Take this: all I have.” And he embraces him.

title: “I do not turn away one who asks”
text: Kicked from the council for saying “Give her back”, Vibhishana crosses the sea with four companions and hangs in the sky above the monkey camp: “I am Ravana’s brother. I have left sons and wife; I come to Rama for refuge.” Sugriva wants him killed as a spy. Rama hears everyone, then: “If a man comes to me once and says ‘I am yours’, I give him safety from all beings. That is my vow. Even if it were Ravana.”

title: The ocean yields
text: For three nights Rama lies on darbha grass by the shore, his arm for a pillow, asking the Ocean for passage. The Ocean does not show himself. “Lakshmana, patience, forgiveness, soft speech: the virtueless take them for weakness. Bring my bow. The monkeys shall cross on foot over dry sand.” The first arrows set the deep on fire. Then the lord of rivers rises from the midst of his waters, palms joined.

title: Nala’s bridge
text: Nala, son of the gods’ own architect, takes charge. Monkeys by the hundred thousand tear up sala, ashvakarna, bamboo, mango and whole hilltops; they haul them with ropes and machines and throw them in. Fourteen yojanas the first day, twenty the second, then twenty-one, twenty-two, twenty-three. On the fifth day it reaches the far shore: a hundred yojanas, straight as the parting in a woman’s hair.

title: Angada’s last warning
text: Before the first arrow, Rama follows the law of kings and sends an envoy. Angada leaps the wall into Ravana’s hall: “I am Vali’s son. Give back Vaidehi and bow to Rama, or the world will be without rakshasas and Vibhishana will rule here.” Four guards seize his arms. He lets them hang on, springs to the palace roof, shakes them off like birds, kicks down the golden pinnacle, shouts his name and is gone.

title: Serpent arrows, and Garuda
text: On the first night of battle Indrajit, invisible by sorcery, shoots arrows that are snakes. They bind Rama and Lakshmana in every limb and the brothers lie still on a bed of shafts. Sita is flown over the field in the Pushpaka to see. Then a wind rises, the sea heaves, and Garuda arrives in a blaze of gold. The serpents flee at his shadow. He strokes the brothers’ faces with his wings and they stand, whole.

title: Kumbhakarna wakes
text: Ravana, beaten from the field, orders his brother woken: six months asleep under Brahma’s curse. They sound conches, beat him with clubs, drive elephants over him, and pile up meat and vats of blood for when he stirs. He tells Ravana plainly that he was wrong, then goes to fight for him anyway. He strides over the wall scooping monkeys into his mouth, until Rama’s arrows take his arms, his legs, and his head.

title: The mountain of herbs
text: Indrajit’s Brahma-weapon lays the whole army low, Rama and Lakshmana with it. In the dark Jambavan asks only one thing: “Does Hanuman live? Then we all may. Go to Himalaya, between the peaks Rishabha and Kailasa. Four herbs grow on the hill there, shining.” The herbs hide from him. So he tears up the whole summit and brings it back through the night, and the scent alone raises the fallen.

title: Lakshmana and Indrajit
text: Vibhishana knows where his nephew gets his invisibility: a rite under a banyan at Nikumbhila. He leads Lakshmana there before it can be finished. Three days and nights they fight, uncle shouting advice, Hanuman carrying the prince. At last Lakshmana fits Indra’s arrow and speaks over it: “If Rama, Dasharatha’s son, is righteous, true to his word and unrivalled in valour, kill Ravana’s son.” It does.

title: Rama and Ravana
text: The gods will not watch Rama fight on foot. Indra’s charioteer Matali brings down the chariot with its green horses, the armour, and the great bow. Then the two go at each other so that the sea stands still and the sun turns pale. There is nothing to compare it to: sky is like sky, ocean like ocean, the battle of Rama and Ravana like the battle of Rama and Ravana. Heads fall and grow back, a hundred times.

title: Enmity ends with death
text: The arrow Brahma made, with the wind in its feathers and the sun in its tip, enters Ravana’s heart, passes through, and returns to the quiver. The bow drops from his hand. Mandodari comes: “You conquered the three worlds, and then your own senses conquered you.” Vibhishana hesitates to perform the rites for such a man. Rama: “Hostility ends at death. Our purpose is done. He is now as much mine as yours.”

title: The fire gives her back
text: Before everyone, Rama says cruel things: that he fought for his name, that she has lived in another man’s house. Sita answers him with dignity and asks Lakshmana to build a pyre. She walks into it. The gods descend; Brahma tells Rama who he is. And the Fire rises in a body, carrying her unburnt, her garland fresh: “Here is your Vaidehi. There is no fault in her.” “I knew,” Rama says. “The world had to see.”

title: The king comes home
text: The Pushpaka carries them north over the bridge, Kishkindha, Panchavati, Chitrakuta; Rama names each place for Sita as it passes. At Nandigrama Bharata, thin in bark, sets the sandals back on his brother’s feet. Vasishtha pours the water of four seas. Sita gives Hanuman her own pearl necklace. And for the years of Rama’s rule, the poet says, no widow wept, no one feared sickness or thieves, the rains came on time, and the old did not have to bury the young.
